At the Thursday cattle market outside the kasba, Wasim sold three goats before noon and felt nothing. Last night his son Faiz, fifteen, had pushed away the mutton curry and said quietly, 'Abbu, I don't want to eat meat anymore. And I don't want to trade goats.'
Wasim had walked out without a word.
On the bus home he sat beside Mahima, the schoolteacher from the next lane. 'Three generations,' he said. 'And he looks at our work like it's wrong.'
'Did you ask him why?'
He hadn't.
That evening he found Faiz feeding the young goat by the shed. Wasim sat on an upturned bucket. 'Tell me. From the start. I'll listen first.'
Faiz talked for a long time, about the goats' faces, about a veterinary course in the city. Wasim felt fear in his chest, and a strange pride too, at how carefully his boy had thought.

qa.q: What did Faiz push away at dinner?
qa.a: The mutton curry.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Wasim have while Faiz talked by the shed?
qa.a: He felt fear in his chest and also a strange pride at how carefully his son had thought it through.

qa.q: What turning point sent Wasim back to talk with Faiz?
qa.a: Mahima's question 'Did you ask him why?' made him see he hadn't, so he chose to sit down and listen first.

qa.q: How might Faiz have felt when his father walked out without a word?
qa.a: Faiz may have felt rejected and worried that his father saw the choice as an insult to three generations of family work.

grounding: Shows a father whose teenage son chooses values and a path he did not expect, feeling fear and pride, and choosing to listen before responding.

passage: With forty relatives coming for Eid lunch and the biryani half-cooked, Ayesha chose that morning to tell her mother. "Ammi, I've stopped eating meat. For three months, actually. For the animals, and the climate." Seema stood still, ladle in hand. Her first feeling was fear: what would Khala say? Then something like grief: this biryani was her own mother's recipe, the dish of every family Eid. She wanted to snap, "Not today." Instead she turned down the flame. "Tell me why. I've got ten minutes." Ayesha talked, fast and nervous, about videos and her science project. Seema listened. And under the worry she felt, oddly, proud: her daughter had thought this through alone. "We'll make a vegetable pulao too," she said. "And you can explain it to Khala yourself."

passage: Vikas had always pictured his daughter Vandana in a chartered accountant's office, like him, only higher up. So when she said at dinner in their Lucknow flat, "Papa, I want to study agriculture. I want to work with farmers on water," he laughed, then saw she wasn't joking. Fear came first: no stable job, the heat, the villages. Then a strange sadness, as if a picture had been taken off the wall. He almost said, "Absolutely not." He pushed his plate away instead. "Explain it to me. From the start." She did: the summer at her nani's village, the dried-up well, a talk by a soil scientist. He listened till the tea went cold. "I'm scared for you," he admitted. "And I'm proud you care about something this much."

qa.q: What does Vandana want to study?
qa.a: Agriculture.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Vikas have after Vandana's announcement?
qa.a: He felt fear about her future, sadness at losing the picture he'd held, and pride in how much she cared.

qa.q: What did Vikas do instead of saying "Absolutely not"?
qa.a: He pushed his plate away and asked her to explain from the start, listening till the tea went cold.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel when her father admits being both scared and proud?
qa.a: Vandana likely feels relieved and respected, knowing he heard her even though he worries.

grounding: Illustrates a father facing his daughter's unexpected career choice with fear, grief and pride, and listening first.

"Amma, I don't want to do the thread ceremony next month."
Irawati set down the invitation list. "Tarun. The priest is booked. Your Ajji is coming from Mysore."
"I know. That's why I'm telling you now."
"Is it because of your friends?"
"No. I've been reading. I'm not sure what I believe. It would feel like lying to wear it."
Irawati looked at the list for a long time. "Your Appa wore it. His father wore it."
"I know, Amma."
She breathed out slowly. "Tell me what you've been reading. All of it. I want to understand before I say anything else."
"Really?"
"I'm scared, Tarun. And sad. But I'm also proud you won't pretend." She pulled out a chair. "Sit. Start from the beginning."

qa.a: Tarun's Ajji.

qa.a: She feels scared and sad about the break in tradition, and proud that Tarun won't pretend.

I still remember the evening, two years ago now, when Karthik put his engineering entrance forms on the table and said, "Appa, I don't want to do this. I want to study music."
My first feeling was fear. I thought of rent, of relatives asking questions, of him struggling at thirty. Then something like grief, for the future I had imagined for him since he was small. I almost said, "No, and that's final."
Instead I said, "Tell me why."
He talked for an hour. About how he felt most himself at the veena. About his teacher saying he had a real ear. About a music college with a teaching diploma, so he could earn.
I didn't agree that night. But I listened. Last month I watched him play at a sabha, eyes closed, and I felt a pride so strong it surprised me.
Shankar

qa.q: What instrument does Karthik play?
qa.a: The veena.

qa.q: What did Shankar feel when Karthik said he wanted to study music?
qa.a: He felt fear about money and Karthik's future, and grief for the future he had imagined for his son.

qa.q: What did Shankar do that kept the relationship intact?
qa.a: He asked "Tell me why" and listened for an hour before responding, instead of saying no straight away.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt when his father asked "Tell me why"?
qa.a: Karthik probably felt nervous but relieved and taken seriously, which let him explain his reasons, including the teaching diploma.

grounding: Shows a father facing his son's choice of music over engineering, feeling fear, grief and later pride, and choosing to listen first.
